leading_positions.synthesis: All eight round-1 files list B001 (optical lattice clocks) as the single part of the preferred configuration, with the same two laureates, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Four members (Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson) state that they moved to B001 from a different opening first place; Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce kept it first. What is shared: the scheme is a distinct many-atom magic-wavelength idea, performance near 10^-18 is reproduced and compared across laboratories, and consequences such as millimetre-to-centimetre gravitational redshift, constants and dark-matter searches are checkable. What is not shared: the citation wording (some stress the lattice concept or magic-wavelength trapping, others the 10^-18 level, others new tests of fundamental physics), how much weight to give the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should affect timing. Nobody proposes a configuration with more than one part, although several raise a two-part prize as an open question. Members name the following as alternatives, which are not part of their preferred configuration: B042 (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce), B017 (Danielsson, Eriksson, Lindroth, Olsson), B003 (Johansson, Kroll, Pearce), and one member each for B045 (Danielsson), B010 (Eriksson), B006 and B004 (Mehlig), and B015 (Olsson).

areas_of_agreement: All eight members put B001 alone in their preferred configuration with the laureate pair Katori and Ye, and nobody argues that a third name is needed.
Members agree that the physics is established and reproduced by independent laboratories, so the result is not a single-laboratory claim.

Members agree that the citation should name the optical lattice (magic-wavelength) clock concept and its realisation, not clocks or precision in general, so as to limit overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks.

Several members (Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) describe the consequences as concrete and checkable: gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres, searches for varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and relativistic geodesy.

Members who comment on B003 (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce, Danielsson) agree it is clean physics but cite proximity to the 2025 prize and a four-name allocation problem as reasons not to place it ahead of B001 this year.
scientific_disputes: Whether the lattice clock is a new discovery or a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes. All eight raise this as the strongest objection; Eriksson, Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce answer that the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme is a distinct principle, while no one has shown the objection to be settled.

Whether a headline uncertainty of 10^-18 counts as a discovery about nature or as a record in systematic control (raised by Olsson), and how much weight the demonstrated new-physics consequences should carry.

For B006, Mehlig (its only opening supporter) acknowledges that the hexatic evidence is system dependent and that some melting transitions are first order; Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll, Olsson and Pearce respond that this and the overlap with the 2016 prize weaken its case, and Olsson adds that the mandate requires experimental verification.

Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene (B017) is a maturity or a scientific objection; Mehlig, Eriksson, Johansson and Danielsson say it argues for waiting, while four members still list B017 as an alternative.
attribution_disputes: All eight name the same two laureates for B001, but Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce each note that other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell, and the Paris, NIST/Boulder and PTB teams) made decisive contributions that a two-name credit leaves out. Several members state they have not verified the priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium experiments.

B042 has five credited names (Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger) and the opening proposals chose three differently (for example Bloch, Greiner, Zoller versus Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger); Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth call this the main difficulty for a prize.

B003 has four credited names for three places, and the proposals differ on the fourth: Girvin appears only in Olsson's proposal, while Blais appears in the others; Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce all flag this.

B015 splits between the 1995 room-temperature discovery (Miyazaki, Moodera) and the later MgO-barrier step (Parkin, with Yuasa, Djayaprawira and Butler-Mathon theory outside the credited names); Eriksson, Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce ask which step would be honoured. Julliere's 1975 precursor is also noted.

B010 versus B004 are overlapping framings of topological insulators with different laureate sets (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp versus Kane, Molenkamp, Xue); Eriksson and Mehlig note that credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan is genuinely split, which the three-person cap cannot represent.

B002 credits three detector conceivers and spokespersons for work by thousands; Pearce, Kroll, Danielsson and Mehlig comment on this limit, and the discovery-year leaders and accelerator builders are excluded.
B045 omits van Paradijs and Piro, according to Danielsson and Olsson.
maturity_disputes: Timing of B001 relative to the redefinition of the SI second: Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce all flag it, and Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce explicitly say the prize should not wait for it, treating it as a metrological decision that follows the physics. Johansson and Olsson list it as an open timing question, and no one has asked to postpone B001 on that basis.

B003 is close in time to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits; Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce say a second circuit prize so soon would look repetitive, while Johansson moved it from first place to an alternative.
B017 is under ten years old and its pairing mechanism is open (Mehlig, Eriksson, Johansson, Danielsson), while Olsson values it as a new platform for controlling phenomena.
B015 is very mature, with about thirty years of confirmation and industrial use, but follows the 2007 GMR prize closely.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson discloses a specific connection to B003 (superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, direction of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, colleagues in the field) and states he should recuse himself from deliberating on B003.
Kroll notes that his WACQT role at Chalmers overlaps with Johansson's institution, relevant only to superconducting-circuit candidates such as B003.

Lindroth discloses a close collaboration with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and co-authorship with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and a field-level connection to B001 and B042, but names no credited person on the shortlist.

Eriksson discloses field-level proximity to the condensed-matter candidates (B010, B017) through his electronic-structure group, with no known collaboration with credited persons, and notes the risk that moving off his own first choice reflects a wish for consensus.
Pearce (chair) discloses that his own fields (astroparticle physics and particle detectors) are adjacent to B045 and B002, with no known tie to the credited persons.
Danielsson, Mehlig and Olsson state that no specific conflict is apparent.
questions_for_round2: Does the committee accept B001 as a distinct discovery from the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes, and what citation wording should state the lattice concept so that it does not claim optical clocks in general?

Is a two-name credit for Katori and Ye defensible given the contributions of other lattice-clock groups, and can anyone with relevant expertise or an external reviewer confirm the priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the 10^-18 result?
Should the pending redefinition of the SI second affect the timing of B001, or is it a metrological step that follows the physics, as Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce argue?

Does any member want to add a second part to the configuration, and if so which of B042, B003, B017 or another alternative, given that none was placed in any member's preferred configuration this round?
For B042, which three of Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger would the committee defend, and is the theory-versus-experiment split resolved by any member's proposal?
For B003, can the committee rule on whether it is too close to the 2025 prize and which fourth name (Girvin or Blais) would be defended, with Johansson recused?
For B015, would the committee honour the 1995 discovery or the MgO step, and can credit be assigned without excluding Yuasa, Djayaprawira or Butler and Mathon?
Does anyone wish to keep B017, B010 or B006 alive, and if so what evidence would resolve the open pairing mechanism, the split topological credit, or the system-dependent hexatic evidence?
summary.chair_observation: All eight round-1 files name B001 alone with Katori and Ye, so the main open issues are the citation wording, whether the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, whether other clock groups are unfairly excluded, and the unverified priority record, not a choice among competing leading proposals. Several members regard the SI second redefinition as a timing question, and four alternatives (B042, B017, B003, B015) each carry a named attribution or maturity problem. This summary counts only positions explicit in the eight files and takes no view on the outcome.
